## Construction

Let $X$ be the metric ray: vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, \ldots$ with edges $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$. The path metric gives $d_X(v_i, v_j) = |i-j|$.

Let $Y$ be the same metric graph: vertices $u_0, u_1, u_2, \ldots$ with edges $[u_{n-1}, u_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$.

Both $X$ and $Y$ have bounded geometry: every edge has length $1$ (bounded above and below), and every vertex has valence at most $2$.

**Definition of $f$.** Set $f(v_n) = u_0$ for all $n \geq 0$. On each edge $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$, parametrized by arclength $t \in [0,1]$, define $f$ to traverse the loop
$$u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n \to u_{n-1} \to \cdots \to u_0$$
at constant speed. This loop has total length $2n$, so the speed is $2n$.

**Cellularity and continuity.** The map sends the $0$-skeleton $X^{(0)}$ into $Y^{(0)}$ (all vertices go to $u_0$) and each $1$-cell into $Y^{(1)} = Y$, so $f$ is cellular. At each vertex $v_n$, both adjacent edges map to loops based at $u_0 = f(v_n)$, so $f$ is continuous.

**$f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is $L$-Lipschitz with $L = 0$.** For any vertices $v_i, v_j$:
$$d_Y(f(v_i), f(v_j)) = d_Y(u_0, u_0) = 0 \leq 0 \cdot d_X(v_i, v_j).$$

**$f$ is not $L'$-Lipschitz for any $L' < \infty$.** On edge $e_n$ (length $1$), the image loop has length $2n$, parametrized at constant speed $2n$. Let $x_n$ be the midpoint of $e_n$ (arclength $t = \tfrac{1}{2}$), which maps to $u_n$ (the midpoint of the loop at arclength $n$). Let $y_n$ be at arclength $t = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4n}$, which maps to the point at arclength $n + \tfrac{1}{2}$ on the return path—i.e., distance $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from $u_n$. Then:
$$d_X(x_n, y_n) = \frac{1}{4n}, \qquad d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n)) = \frac{1}{2},$$
so the ratio is
$$\frac{d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n))}{d_X(x_n, y_n)} = 2n \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} \infty.$$
For any $L' < \infty$, choosing $n > L'/2$ yields a pair violating the $L'$-Lipschitz condition. Hence $f$ is not Lipschitz for any finite constant.

**Non-degenerate variant ($L = 1$).** Set $f(v_n) = u_n$ and map each edge $[v_{n-1}, v_n]$ to the path $u_{n-1} \to u_{n-2} \to \cdots \to u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n$ of length $(n-1) + n = 2n - 1$, parametrized at constant speed. Then $f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is the identity on the ray, hence $1$-Lipschitz, while the slope on $e_n$ is $2n - 1 \to \infty$, so $f$ is not Lipschitz.

**Key point.** A cellular map between graphs need only send vertices to vertices; on each edge it is an arbitrary continuous path in the target graph. The $0$-skeleton Lipschitz condition constrains only the images of vertices, leaving the behavior on edge interiors (which can traverse arbitrarily long paths) completely unconstrained.

### PROOF COMPLETE

**Construction.**

Let $X$ be the metric graph obtained from a ray: vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, \ldots$ with edges $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$. The path metric gives $d_X(v_i, v_j) = |i - j|$.

Let $Y$ be the same metric graph: vertices $u_0, u_1, u_2, \ldots$ with edges $[u_{n-1}, u_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$.

Both $X$ and $Y$ have bounded geometry: all edges have length $1$ (bounded above and below), and every vertex has valence at most $2$.

Define $f: X \to Y$ as follows:
- On vertices: $f(v_n) = u_0$ for all $n \geq 0$.

## Construction

Let $X$ be the metric ray: vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, \ldots$ with edges $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$. The path metric gives $d_X(v_i, v_j) = |i-j|$.

Let $Y$ be the same metric graph: vertices $u_0, u_1, u_2, \ldots$ with edges $[u_{n-1}, u_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$.

Both $X$ and $Y$ have bounded geometry: every edge has length $1$ (bounded above and below), and every vertex has valence at most $2$.

**Definition of $f$.** Set $f(v_n) = u_0$ for all $n \geq 0$. On each edge $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$, parametrized by arclength $t \in [0,1]$, define $f$ to traverse the loop
$$u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n \to u_{n-1} \to \cdots \to u_0$$
at constant speed. This loop has total length $2n$, so the speed is $2n$.

**Cellularity and continuity.** The map sends the $0$-skeleton $X^{(0)}$ into $Y^{(0)}$ (all vertices go to $u_0$) and each $1$-cell into $Y^{(1)} = Y$, so $f$ is cellular. At each vertex $v_n$, both adjacent edges map to loops based at $u_0 = f(v_n)$, so $f$ is continuous.

**$f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is $L$-Lipschitz with $L = 0$.** For any vertices $v_i, v_j$:
$$d_Y(f(v_i), f(v_j)) = d_Y(u_0, u_0) = 0 \leq 0 \cdot d_X(v_i, v_j).$$

**$f$ is not $L'$-Lipschitz for any $L' < \infty$.** On edge $e_n$ (length $1$), the image loop has length $2n$, parametrized at constant speed $2n$. Let $x_n$ be the midpoint of $e_n$ (arclength $t = \tfrac{1}{2}$), which maps to $u_n$ (the midpoint of the loop at arclength $n$). Let $y_n$ be at arclength $t = \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{4n}$, which maps to the point at arclength $n + \tfrac{1}{2}$ on the return path—i.e., distance $\tfrac{1}{2}$ from $u_n$. Then:
$$d_X(x_n, y_n) = \frac{1}{4n}, \qquad d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n)) = \frac{1}{2},$$
so the ratio is
$$\frac{d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n))}{d_X(x_n, y_n)} = 2n \xrightarrow{n \to \infty} \infty.$$
For any $L' < \infty$, choosing $n > L'/2$ yields a pair violating the $L'$-Lipschitz condition. Hence $f$ is not Lipschitz for any finite constant.

**Non-degenerate variant ($L = 1$).** Set $f(v_n) = u_n$ and map each edge $[v_{n-1}, v_n]$ to the path $u_{n-1} \to u_{n-2} \to \cdots \to u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n$ of length $(n-1) + n = 2n - 1$, parametrized at constant speed. Then $f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is the identity on the ray, hence $1$-Lipschitz, while the slope on $e_n$ is $2n - 1 \to \infty$, so $f$ is not Lipschitz.

**Key point.** A cellular map between graphs need only send vertices to vertices; on each edge it is an arbitrary continuous path in the target graph. The $0$-skeleton Lipschitz condition constrains only the images of vertices, leaving the behavior on edge interiors (which can traverse arbitrarily long paths) completely unconstrained.

**Construction.**

Let $X$ be the metric graph obtained from a ray: vertices $v_0, v_1, v_2, \ldots$ with edges $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$. The path metric gives $d_X(v_i, v_j) = |i - j|$.

Let $Y$ be the same metric graph: vertices $u_0, u_1, u_2, \ldots$ with edges $[u_{n-1}, u_n]$ of length $1$ for each $n \geq 1$.

Both $X$ and $Y$ have bounded geometry: all edges have length $1$ (bounded above and below), and every vertex has valence at most $2$.

Define $f: X \to Y$ as follows:
- On vertices: $f(v_n) = u_0$ for all $n \geq 0$.
- On each edge $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ (parametrized by arclength $t \in [0, 1]$): $f$ maps $e_n$ to the loop in $Y$ that traverses $u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n \to u_{n-1} \to \cdots \to u_0$, parametrized at constant speed. This loop has total length $2n$.

**Continuity and cellularity.** At each vertex $v_n$, both adjacent edges map to paths starting/ending at $u_0 = f(v_n)$, so $f$ is continuous. Since $f$ maps vertices (the $0$-skeleton) to vertices and edges (the $1$-skeleton) into the $1$-skeleton, $f$ is cellular.

**$f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is $L$-Lipschitz (with $L = 0$).** For any two vertices $v_i, v_j$, we have $f(v_i) = f(v_j) = u_0$, so $d_Y(f(v_i), f(v_j)) = 0 \leq 0 \cdot d_X(v_i, v_j)$. Thus $f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is $0$-Lipschitz.

**$f$ is not $L'$-Lipschitz for any $L' < \infty$.** Consider edge $e_n = [v_{n-1}, v_n]$ of length $1$. The image loop has length $2n$, parametrized at constant speed $2n$ on an interval of length $1$. Take $x_n$ at the midpoint of $e_n$ (arclength $t = 1/2$), which maps to $u_n$ (the midpoint of the loop, at arclength $n$). Take $y_n$ at arclength $t = 1/2 + \frac{1}{4n}$, which maps to the point at arclength $n + \frac{1}{2}$ on the loop (i.e., $\frac{1}{2}$ units past $u_n$ on the return path). Then:
$$d_X(x_n, y_n) = \frac{1}{4n}, \qquad d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n)) = \frac{1}{2}.$$
The ratio is $\frac{d_Y(f(x_n), f(y_n))}{d_X(x_n, y_n)} = 2n \to \infty$ as $n \to \infty$.

Therefore, for any $L' < \infty$, choosing $n > L'/2$ gives a pair $(x_n, y_n)$ violating the $L'$-Lipschitz condition. Hence $f$ is not $L'$-Lipschitz for any finite $L'$.

**Non-degenerate variant.** One can also arrange $f|_{X^{(0)}}$ to be $1$-Lipschitz (not $0$-Lipschitz) by setting $f(v_n) = u_n$ and mapping each edge $[v_{n-1}, v_n]$ to the path $u_{n-1} \to u_{n-2} \to \cdots \to u_0 \to u_1 \to \cdots \to u_n$ (length $2n - 1$). Then $f|_{X^{(0)}}$ is the identity on the ray, hence $1$-Lipschitz, while the slope on edge $e_n$ is $2n - 1 \to \infty$.
